visible.summary:
The UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025) identifies the North Caucasus — including Dagestan — as a zone where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, documenting systematic campaigns by Chechen and North-Caucasus authorities between 2017 and 2024 including abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings. North Caucasus SOS's director states there is “no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus”, that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families, and that the situation worsens year on year.

Canada's travel advisory tells travellers to avoid all travel to Russia, names Dagestan among the republics where terrorist attacks are frequent, and warns that special permission from the Ministry of the Interior is required to enter certain areas — an access regime that also hampers independent monitoring of how state and customary authority operate on the ground.

For a visitor the risk here is the regional pattern: the federal ‘extremist’ designation of 2023, which extended violence in detention beyond the region, combined with local security structures and family-honour norms that produce extrajudicial responses unmediated by legal process. No separate Dagestan-specific written law targeting trans people exists, and no Chechnya-scale documented purge infrastructure is attributed to this republic.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 'no safe life' assessment and the shared security-and-custom enforcement logic concern LGBTIQ+ people broadly rather than tabulating trans-specific cases in the republic.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Advisories cite frequent terrorist attacks and instability across the North Caucasus for all travellers; that general insecurity is distinct from the trans-specific exception the same advisories carve out.

Testimony-based regional assessment underpinning this record's 'no safe private existence' line.

Western travel advisories name the republic within the broader Caucasus don't-travel area. Wikipedia (LGBTQ rights in Russia), the federal framework applying in North Ossetia–Alania: in November 2023 the Russian Supreme Court designated the 'international LGBT public movement' as an extremist group, making participation in LGBT activism illegal. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition outright, prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition, and the federal 'propaganda' law of 2013 was expanded in December 2022 to apply to people of all ages and to materials that make minors interested in gender transition; new laws effective 1 July 2023 effectively reclassify homosexuality as a mental illness. Confirms that visible LGBT activity a visitor brings into the republic sits entirely outside federal legal protection.

visible.summary:
Stavropol Krai is named in the Canadian travel advisory's special-permission requirement (alongside Chechnya, Dagestan, and Ingushetia) and is included in the North Caucasus zone identified by the UK Home Office CPIN as the exception to Russia's general risk picture. The dossier specifically identifies the south-eastern part bordering Chechnya as subject to the same security-and-custom enforcement logic. However, Stavropol is a krai, not a republic, and the extreme documented violence (secret prisons, purges, coerced conscription) is Chechen-specific rather than krai-wide.

For a visitor, the special-permission regime itself restricts movement and independent oversight, and the south-eastern areas adjacent to Chechnya share the localised security culture. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.05 below. Above the core North Caucasus republics (Dagestan, Ingushetia at 0.04; Kabardino-Balkaria, Karachay-Cherkessia, North Ossetia at 0.05) because the extreme evidence is geographically limited to the Chechnya border zone within a large multi-ethnic krai, and no independent republic-level security apparatus analogous to Kadyrov's exists.
visible.tangentialFactors: The Caucasus-zone enforcement logic the dossier documents applies to LGBTIQ+ people broadly; the special-permission and checkpoint culture is not trans-status-specific.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: The special-permission requirement Canada identifies for this krai applies to all foreign travellers regardless of personal characteristic - a movement-control measure whose trans-relevant content is only what it signals about the security apparatus near the Chechnya border; the advisory zone itself reflects general insecurity.

visible.summary:
Moscow is where the federal anti-LGBT framework is enforced most visibly. The Moscow Times' 2025 survey of persecution — headlined around “arrests, club raids and extremism charges” — records that the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds, Kotov, was arrested in Moscow in late December 2024; the paper reported Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-‘extremism’ designation in February 2025, an organising case following a ruling reported from Siberia in January 2025.

The severity of the federal law is uniform across the country, but enforcement intensity is not: Moscow concentrates the highest police density, the most active venue-level operations, and the bureaucratic touchpoints most likely to involve a foreign visitor — document verification, medical gatekeeping, registration procedures. For a trans visitor the practical result is a materially higher probability of encountering active enforcement of the same rules, and the country offers no protective institutional counterweight at any level.
visible.tangentialFactors: The extremism-designation prosecutions centred on Moscow target organisers and LGBT-facing venues broadly, not only trans people - the general anti-LGBT enforcement climate is part of what a trans-presenting visitor is exposed to.
visible.localsOnly: The medical and bureaucratic gatekeeping the 2023 federal transition ban concentrates here bears on residents navigating transition paperwork and care; a visitor's exposure is enforcement-side (venue raids, document and registration checks, the propaganda-law detention and deportation risk).
visible.outOfScopeNotes: The blanket don't-travel levels (State Department, FCDO) reflect wrongful-detention and war risk for all travellers; they are not trans-specific evidence, though the propaganda-law detention rule embedded in them is.

Wikipedia's Russia country overview records the federal framework a Moscow visitor stands under: the Supreme Court in November 2023 declared the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and on 22 March 2024 it was formally added to the state's unified list of terrorist and extremist organisations, a designation the page says has led to arrests of gay bar owners and of people displaying rainbow-flag symbols on extremism charges. The page also records the July 2023 federal law banning gender transition outright - both gender-affirming surgery and any legal gender recognition - plus Moscow-specific facts: Moscow authorities have never approved a request to hold a gay pride rally, and in 2011 the head of the Moscow Registry Office stated publicly that attempts by same-sex couples to marry in Moscow are "doomed to fail."
